title: Discriminated unions over 'bag of optionals': modeling frontend state in TypeScript
summary: Matt Pocock argues that most frontend complexity comes from handling states, and that handling starts with how states are typed. He contrasts a 'bag of optionals' type, which permits impossible shapes, with a discriminated union that makes each state carry exactly its own data. He also extends the idea to component props.

principles.text: Most frontend complexity is state handling, and handling states starts with how they are represented in types.
principles.quote: Most of the complexity in frontend comes from handling all the various states your app can be in.

principles.text: A 'bag of optionals' type permits impossible states; use optionals only when a value truly may or may not be present.
principles.quote: Optional properties are best used when a value might or might not be present. In this case, that isn't right.

principles.text: Model state as a discriminated union so each status carries exactly the data that exists in that state.
principles.quote: The more accurate way to represent this is using a discriminated union.

principles.text: Build the union by scaffolding the discriminant branches first, then adding each branch's own properties.
principles.quote: Now that we've got our scaffolding, we can start adding elements to each branch of the union.

principles.text: TypeScript's strictness on unions is a feature; it pushes you to think in states and access data only where it exists.
principles.quote: By ensuring you can only access data when the status equals `success`, you're encouraged to think of your app in terms of its states, and only access data in the states it's available.

principles.text: Use discriminated unions for component props when a component renders in different variants, so variant-specific props are required only when relevant.
